audits.title: Inspection of fishery products

recommendations.text: Official Supervision - The Lithuanian competent authority should approve where relevant and strengthen the supervision on the HACCP system put in place into the establishments. - The Lithuanian competent authority should supervise microbiological controls performed by the establishments and should require them to keep adequate records. - Proper practical training for official veterinarians should be provided for.

Establishments/vessels - Upgrading of structure and hygienic conditions should be achieved in all fishing vessels delivering fish and fishery products to the plants approved for export to EU countries, according to the Act signed by the Director of the State Veterinary Service on 8 July 1999. - A list of approved independent cold stores for the storage of fishery products destined to EU countries should be established - Automatic temperature recording in cold stores should be put in place. - General hygienic practices during processing in the fishery establishments should be upgraded (use of hand-operated showers should be avoided). - Establishments should preferably perform official analyses in Lithuanian approved laboratories. 8 of 9
Laboratories The official laboratories should be able to perform TVB-N and TMA-N analyses.

Written assurances Written guarantees should be forwarded to the European Commission in respect of the correction of the points listed above within one month from the date of receipt of the final report. 8.2. For the Commission Services After receiving and evaluating the written assurances sought from the Lithuanian Competent Authority regarding the public health issues, the Commission services should propose to Member States that Lithuania be placed on part I of the Annex to the amended Commission Decision 97/296/EC. 9 of 9

recommendations.text: To the Lithuanian authorities 9.1.1. to take immediate action to remove the game plant establishment visited from the list of EU approved plants14. The re-approval of the establishment should not be considered until the Commission services have reviewed this report and indicated whether the assurances offered are acceptable. 14 This action was taken by the Lithuanian authorities before the end of the mission. 20 9.1.2. to take appropriate action to improve the certification system in place in Lithuania; 9.1.3. to take urgent action to stop the use of raw milk not complying with the requirements of EC legislation in the manufacture of milk and milk products intended for export to EU Member States; 9.1.4. to take appropriate measures to correct the other deficiencies mentioned in this report, and to check that all establishments approved for export to the EU comply with the relevant EC legislative standards. The Lithuanian authorities must prepare an action plan to address both the above general recommendations, and the detailed conclusions of this report. This plan must indicate the deadlines for the implementation and completion of each of the required actions. The plan should be submitted to the Commission's services within one month of receipt of the final report.

To the Commission's services 9.2.1. immediately to remove the game plant visited from the EU list of approved plants, in accordance with the action taken by the Lithuanian Central Competent Authority. audits.title: Animal Welfare

recommendations.text: To ensure that routine tail docking of pigs is not permitted (Directive 91/630/EEC Annex, Chapter I point 8).

Regarding laying hen holdings: (a) To complete the registration of holdings with the information required in the Annex of Directive 2002/4/EC. (b) To ensure that holdings with more than 350 hens meet the requirements of Directive 99/74/EC, in particular the cage specifications. (c) To ensure that a distinguishing number is stamped on the egg as required by point 2 of the Annex of Directive 2002/4/EC. (d) To enforce the prohibition on forced moulting of laying hens (point 15 and 16 of the Annex of Council Directive 98/58/EC).
Regarding transporters: to ensure that the system in place allows the rapid identification of international transporters (Council Directive 91/628/EEC Chapter II, Article 5 A, 1a).
Regarding route plans: to ensure that (a) Journey times are verified. (b) Route plans are returned after the journey.

Regarding surveillance in slaughterhouses: to ensure that (a) Restraint facilities are appropriate to the stunning equipment (Annex B of Council Directive 93/119/EC). (b) Electrodes of devices used to stun animals span the brain (Council Directive 93/119/EC Annex C, II.3.A1). 8 9. ADDENDUM TO MISSION REPORT DG(SANCO)/7306/2004 In their comments on a draft version of this report, the CCA provided the following initial reaction to the recommendations: (1) Routine tail docking of pigs is not permitted, except in cases when this procedure is needed for animal health reasons. (2) Regarding laying hen holdings: (a) The register of the laying hen holdings is updated with the information required in the Annex of Directive 2002/4/EC. (c) Currently distinguishing number is stamped on the egg as required by point 2 of the Annex of Directive 2002/4/EC. (d) Forced moulting of laying hens is prohibited in the Republic of Lithuania. Veterinary inspectors are instructed to check strictly the system of water supply to the cages where laying hens are kept. (3) By the Order of the Director of SFVS of 10 June 2004 all subjects, including animal transporters are currently undergoing veterinary approval procedure and will be included into the Register, which is available at the web site of SFVS. (4) County and district SFVS are obliged to approve the route plans only if they are appropriately completed. In the case of non return, a letter has to be sent to the transporter and, if necessary, further export shall be prohibited. SFVS is strengthening the control under the management of route plans. Food and Veterinary Audit Service on the regular basis performs controls on all activities (including approval of route plans) of SFVS. (5) Regarding surveillance in slaughterhouses: (a) The SFVS is monitoring the proper restraint of animals before stunning. (b) By the Order of SFVS of 5 July 2004 inappropriate devices for electrical stunning of cattle were prohibited. The new questionnaires for the inspections of slaughterhouses approved by the Order of SFVS of 31 August 2004, ensures that inappropriate devices for electrical stunning of cattle are not used. 9

recommendations.text: Ensure that sample preparation for the analysis of aflatoxins complies with Commission Directive 98/53/EC.
Ensure inspection of premises handling at risk products are carried out to assess potential food hazards associated with the business, specifically controls on aflatoxins.
Proceed towards full validation of analytical methods for irradiated foods, sudan dyes, 3-MCPD and mycotoxins.
Ensure that analytical results are reported adjusted for recovery/uncertainty or stating the rate of recovery and uncertainty.

To ensure that all animal movements, including those passing through markets and dealers premises are notified and that all data are communicated within the legal deadlines and promptly entered in the CDB.
To issue instructions and guidance for the OV on how to proceed when animal identification requirements of Regulation (EC) 1760/2000 are not fulfilled.

To ensure that OVs in red meat establishments have a thorough understanding of the importance of analysing and cross-checking the results of operators' own check programmes and to initiate corrective action when needed in accordance with Council Directive 64/433/EEC and the HACCP provisions laid down in Commission Decision 2001/476/EC.
To enforce controls to ensure the correct application of Regulation (EC) 1774/2002.
To enforce controls regarding the correct use of health and identification marks in accordance with the legal requirements.

To ensure the full application of the national monitoring programme for brucellosis in cattle and sheep by improving awareness among farmers to 1 Council Directives 2003/85/EC, 2001/89/EC, 92/40/EEC, and 92/66/EEC. 18 notify abortions and to ensure that the follow-up will be done according to Council Directive 64/432/EEC.

audits.title: Pesticides

recommendations.text: The competent authorities should continue with the revision of the labels to ensure that all labels of PPPs are in compliance with Directive 1999/45/EC of the European Parliament and the Council on classification, packaging and labelling of dangerous preparations.
The competent authorities should arrange to finalise the destruction of obsolete pesticides in order to avoid possible contamination of food, feed and the environment. 20
The competent authorities should commence sampling and analysis to ensure the implementation of Commission Directives 91/321/EEC and 96/5/EC on foodstuffs for infants and young children, as amended.

The competent authorities should consider increasing the range of pesticides and metabolites in the analytical screens, so as to better reflect those substances being marketed and to ensure adequate enforcement of pesticide MRLs as specified in Council Directives 76/895/EEC, 86/362/EEC and 90/642/EEC as amended, and taking account of the Recommendation of the EU co-ordinated monitoring programme.

The competent authorities should consider taking full account of the Quality Control Procedures for Pesticide Residues Analysis Document No. SANCO/10476/2003, particularly with respect to calibration.
The competent authorities should continue with the review of authorisation of PPPs to comply with the new MRL when MRLs change.

The laboratory should consider taking measures to avoid possible cross- contamination between standards and samples. An action plan in response to the recommendations should be forwarded to the Commission within 2 months of dispatch of the final translated report. This action plan should clearly set out the manner and deadline by which the competent authorities will address each recommendation. 9. ADDENDUM In the response to the draft report, the Lithuanian Competent Authorities provided a number of corrections and comments, and provided comments o s number 2, 3, 4 and 5. In relation to recommendation no 2 the Ministry of Environment stated that they plan to dispose the remaining stocks of obsolete pesticides by the end of 2005. In relation to recommendation no 3, 4 and 5 the State Food and Veterinary Service stated that they propose the following actions: Regardi No. 3, the Draft Food Contamination Monitoring Program for 2006 has been prepared, which includes testing of 10 samples of foodstuffs for infants and young children (8 samples from the market, 2 samples on imports). Regardi No. 4, the National Veterinary Laboratory has purchased a new GC-MS system; installation is going on and it is planned to start analysis of pesticide residues using this system by the end of 2005. The system will be used for routine analysis from the beginning of 2006. According to agreement with the company, the new LC-MS/MS system will be purchased and installed in December 2005 ­ January 2006. The new facilities will allow to increase the range of pesticides and metabolites and ensure enforcement of pesticide MRLs as specified in Council Directives 76/895/EEC, 86/362/EEC and 90/642/EEC and 21 taking account of the Recommendation of the EU co-ordinated monitoring programme. Regardi No. 5, most of requirements of SANCO/10476/2003 are applied to analysis of one group of pesticide residues (organophosphorus and organo-nitrogen compounds, which are analysed by Gas chromatograph with nitrogen-phosphorus detector ­ GC-NPD). These requirements will be applied to other groups of pesticides in 2006. 22

recommendations.text: To extend the scope of testing under the NRCP to include all necessary substance groups in accordance with Annex II to Council Directive 96/23/EC and to expand the scope of analyses (i.e. the number of compounds analysed for within each compound group) in order to maximise the possibility of detecting residues in accordance with paragraphs 2 and 3 of Annex III to Council Directive 96/23/EC.

To improve the reporting system and information exchange between each of the relevant authorities in order to improve supervision of the implementation of the NRCP in accordance with Article 4 of Council Directive 96/23/EC.

To continue monitoring `at risk' products for the presence of chloramphenicol and strengthen efforts to eliminate the occurrence of this substance in raw milk and dairy products.
To ensure that analytical methods used for the NRCP comply with validation requirements established in Community law (Commission Decision 2002/657/EC).

To provide a detailed timetable indicating milestones and deadlines for the development of analytical methods, their validation according to Commission Decision 2002/657/EC and their introduction into the 2006 NRCP. 9. audits.title: Food Hygiene - Food of animal origin

recommendations.text: To ensure access for the OVs to update information about official controls and to improve knowledge at central level about the applied approach of the controls at the county level.

To update procedures and instructions in particular as regards definitions applied for different types of official control to bring them all fully in line with the provisions of Regulations (EC) 882/2004 and 854/2004 respectively.

To improve and further develop the risk assessment applied with the aim of increasing the diversification of control frequencies of similar types or establishments displaying different risks in the national official control programme as the basis for establishing control frequencies. 19

To strengthen the official control of EU-non-compliant third country animal products in order to ensure full compliance in all cases with the requirements of Commission Decision 2005/571/EC, Article 11 (2)(d) of Council Directive 97/78/EC and Article 12 of Regulation 854/2004 respectively.

To ensure the issuing of accurate approvals reflecting all activities carried out by the food businesses in line with Article 4 of Regulation (EC) 853/2004 and Article 3 of Regulation (EC) 854/2004 respectively.
To strengthen the audits on HACCP-based procedures and verification of the compliance in all cases with the requirements of Regulation (EC) 2073/2005.
To apply a health mark for emergency slaughtered animals with a format that fully ensures that the requirements of Annex III, Section I, Chapter 9 of Regulation (EC) 853/2004 will be complied with.
To organise the system of official control of dairy farms in a way that ensures immediate suspension of milk deliveries when required by the legislation.

To ensure that proper risk assessment and definition of period of acceptance in line with the requirements of Article 5 of Regulation (EC) 852/2004, Chapter II(II)(2)(a) of Annex III of Regulation (EC) 853/2004 and Article 12 of Regulation (EC) 2076/2005 are established.

To ensure the correct application of all the approval requirements of Article 12 (4)(b) of Council Directive 97/78/EC with regard to warehouses. Legislation New legislation and implementing provisions were issued to address the recommendations issued with mission report 7676/2005, in line with the commitments made by Lithuania before the Standing Committee in December 2005. A correct meaning of "other fields" as mentioned in Council Directive 93/85/EEC has been introduced by the Order No 3D-87 and implemented consistently, addressing Recommendation (2) of report DG(SANCO)7676/2005. 7.2. Plant health system in Lithuania The SPPS headquarters has a good level of control of the activities performed for potato controls. Inspectors met were competent and acquainted with the new provisions on potato controls. A good level of awareness of producers, wholesalers and managers of packing stations on ring rot issues was noted during the on-the-spot visits. Activities on potato controls are carried out consistently in the regions visited. 7.3. Seed potatoes in Lithuania Plant passports for seed potatoes are now being issued; labels and information contained are in compliance with Commission Directive 92/105/EEC. The potato genetic material originating in Third Countries detained by the Lithuanian Institute of Agriculture will be tested in 2007 for all the organisms mentioned in Commission Directive 95/44/EC, before its release, as requested by Recommendation (6). Checks are performed by the SPPS where seed potatoes are traded for the presence of the plant passport. 7.4. Potatoes other than seed All potato growers who want to trade their production need to be registered with the SPPS, as well as packing stations and wholesalers. The number of registered producers has almost doubled since last mission. The registration of producers is still in progress. 18 Handling of ring rot outbreaks is done in compliance with the requirements of Council Directive 93/85/EC: procedures, demarcation of zones and official measures are applied consistently, as requested by Recommendation (1). The incidence of the disease has increased compared to previous year: this is mainly due to the inclusion of small farms in the national survey. Quarantine measures applied following an outbreak are compulsory and if necessary are enforced, addressing Recommendation (3). The legal owners of fields subject to quarantine measures are informed about the measures imposed on them following an occurrence of a quarantine organism, as requested by Recommendation (4). Labels attached to ware potatoes include a registration number in accordance with the requirements of point 18.5 of Annex IV, part A, Section II to Council Directive 2000/29/EC, and as indicated by Recommendation (5). A list of varieties accepted as being resistant to potato wart disease and potato cyst nematode was sent by Lithuania to the Commission, in compliance with Article 10 of Council Directives 69/464/EEC and 69/465/EEC, as requested by Recommendation (7). Non registered producers are included in the surveys and controls for ring rot, addressing Advisory point (9). Occasional checks are performed by the SPPS at open markets to check for compliance with the provisions for labelling. 7.5. Laboratories Despite the fact that the new laboratory will only be completed later this year, the number of analyses performed for ring rot has increased substantially. The density of laboratory testing for ring rot has been increased and includes farm saved seed, as indicated in Advisory point (8). The requirements for water sampling for potato brown rot testing is now in line with the ones in the note on included sampling in the proposed amendment to Council Directive 98/57/EC14 , as requested by Advisory point (10). 7.6. Recommendation from report DG(SANCO)7261/2005 Recommendations (3) and (4) issued with mission report DG(SANCO)7261/2005 have been satisfactorily addressed. 14 SANCO/1191/2004 Rev. 9 (PVNA/2004/1191/1191R9-EN.doc) 19 8. OVERALL CONCLUSION The actions taken for the control of potato ring rot, disease caused by the bacterium Clavibacter michiganensis ssp. sepedonicus, are now in compliance with those established in Council Directive 93/85/EC. Procedures were found to be implemented homogeneously throughout the country. Official measures and disposal of contaminated potatoes are done under the supervision of the State Plant Protection Service. Plant passport for seed potatoes is now being issued. All recommendations of the report DG(SANCO)7676/2005 and recommendations (3) and (4) of mission report DG(SANCO)7261/2004 have been satisfactorily addressed. 9. recommendations.text: The legal order issued on 31/07/2007 which bans the transport of horses for slaughter for more than eight hours and authorises the journey to be extended by four hours if horses are to be slaughtered in a slaughterhouse located in another Member State is modified so it complies with Regulation (EC) No 1/2005.

recommendations.text: ure that all operators active along the chain of ABP/DP, namely transporters, are registered before commencing operations as required by Article 23 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009.

citations.text: As regards transporters, the audit team noted that in some cases the transporters indicated on the commercial documents were not identical to the ones indicated on the CMR way bill. Some of the transporters mentioned on the CMR way bills seen by the audit team during the visits to operators were not registered as ABP transporters.

In the pet food plant visited, an inspector had identified during a previous official control that a transporter used by a supplier was not a registered ABP operator. The pet food plant was requested to stop using this transporter. The audit team noted that this approach does not prevent the transporter from continuing to transport ABP for other operators without being registered. The inspector confirmed that this transporter was never used again to deliver products to the pet food plant, however, he could not say whether the transporter is now registered as an ABP operator or not.

In one of the paper traders visited, the audit team noted that the operator engaged in the trade of ABP/DP before being registered by the competent authorities; three consignments 5 were traded prior to becoming registered. According to the trader, the trading partners were the ones to highlight the obligation to be registered (see paragraph 17). 5.1.3 Organisation, planning and execution of official controls

The competent authorities have the necessary elements to maintain and implement a system of official controls as required by Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 which is enhanced by the implementation of the quality management system in place for official controls and the good co-operation and co-ordination between SFVS and territorial SFVS; however, the effectiveness of the system is negatively affected by a number of transporters or traders not being registered as ABP operators before engaging into activities in the ABP/DP chain and consequently not being controlled. citations.text: The audit team noted that the competent authority made available to the staff of the BIPs visited the procedures related to transit movements (i.e. controls of transits at entry and exit BIPs and at Customs warehouses). The available procedures were up-to-date in the BIPs visited and staff also has access to the internal IT network of the competent authority which includes the entire documented system for the official import controls. 3 This is used by staff in order to be kept up-to-date in the area of their competence as required by Article 6(b) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The audit team noted the following exceptions: a. previous FVO audit report (2013-6962) recommended that the competent authority develop the procedure in order to ensure that BIP staff is up-to-date on the specific provisions applicable to transits of live animals. The competent authority stated that this was under review and provided the draft version to the audit team. b. there was no procedure for the controls of external transits. BFVCD is the competent authority responsible but has not planned the controls of external transits, which are required by Article 6(1) of Directive 89/662/EEC. Those controls would aim at preventing that EU goods transiting via third countries with specific animal health risks re-enter the Union. However, due to geographical position and the trade patterns of Lithuania, those movements are limited. The audit team did not find evidence of such movements in TRACES and the competent authority confirmed this during the audit.

The competent authority has implemented the requirements for communication, cooperation and training to support the overall functioning of the controls on transits, except in regard of transits of live animals (which was a recommendation of the 2013 FVO audit) and controls on external transits (which are not included in the planning of controls).

The competent authority stated that the port and rail BIPs visited conduct manifest checks (with a view to identifying possible cases of consignments not presented at the BIPs) on an ad hoc basis and there is no recording of these controls. The road BIP visited does not monitor incoming consignments in order to identify cases that should be subject to veterinary controls, contrary to the requirements of Article 7 of Regulation (EC) 136/2004 and Article 6 of Regulation (EC) 282/2004. The audit team noted that the procedure for controls of transits does not refer to the above-mentioned requirements. 5.2.1.2 Veterinary checks

In particular it is not clear when the BIP staff need to perform a full identity check and whether consignments that have been rejected should leave the BIP sealed (a case was noted in which the rail BIP performed a full identity check on a consignment and rejected it unsealed). The above may lead to a lack of consistency in the related controls among the different BIPs.

recommendations.text: To ensure that when any level of unauthorised substance is found in organic products or fields, adequate investigations are carried out and immediate action taken to prevent fraudulent use of organic indications in line with Article 91 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Recommendation is based upon conclusions No 4, 65 and 92

citations.text: The audit team noted that there is a clause in the national rules on organic agriculture on response to positive laboratory results that is not in line with EU legislation. See paragraph 62 below. There were also a limited number of other discrepancies with EU legislation in the implementation of the Lithuanian control system, caused either by incorrect or absence of guidance in the relevant Orders or by incorrect interpretation. These discrepancies are detailed in the relevant sections of the report. Conclusions on relevant national legislation and provisions

As stipulated in the national Rules on Organic Agriculture, Ekoagros applies a threshold for detected unauthorised substances below which, no contamination is recorded or investigation or other follow-up carried out. The threshold is formally 0.01 mg/kg, but since the measurement of uncertainty, which the laboratory is obliged to indicate (generally 50%), must also be added the threshold is in practice most often 0.02 mg/kg. Furthermore, this still applies if several substances are found, as long as the level of each substance is below the threshold. In 2019-2020, some 40% of the positive samples found in the risk-based surveys were below the threshold and in practice regarded as negative. Paragraph 88 below gives an example of similar effects of the threshold on the follow- up of suspected cases. The application of a threshold is not in line with Article 91 of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Any presence of unauthorised substance is a potential non-compliance with the organic rules and should be investigated. In this context, the uncertainty factor is irrelevant as it applies to the level of contamination and not to whether there is presence or not.

The Rules on Organic Agriculture lay down the overall procedure and rights and obligations regarding particular types of irregularities, such as presence of an unauthorised substance. In cases of the latter, if the level of (each) unauthorised substance is above the threshold (see 62 above), the lot in question is blocked and the operator is given 5 days to request an investigation, for which he has to pay the additional analyses of samples. If the operator does not make such a request the lot is downgraded to conventional and if on a farm, the field is furthermore downgraded to conversion and the farmer loses the subsidy on the field for that year.

Order No 3D-370 of 22 May 2009 describes the procedure for the exchange of information of non-compliances with other Member States and the Commission in the OFIS system. The audit team examined examples of the follow-up done in response to notifications made by other Member States. One of them involved the finding of Glyphosate in oats exported by a grain trader in 2019. The lot was originally composed from 140 truckloads of oats from over 50 farmers. By analysing the samples referred to in paragraph 45 above, Glyphosate was confirmed in 121 of the 140 truckloads. However, after applying the threshold described in paragraph 62 above, only seven samples, involving four farms were considered positive with a need for follow-up. Inspections and sampling, either of remaining grain or of soil from the fields where the oats had been grown, verified Glyphosate contamination in three of the farms. The remaining farms with Glyphosate levels below the threshold in the original sample were not included in risk category I (see paragraph 35 above) for controls in the following 20 year. Ekoagros explained that this principle was not yet in place when this case occurred, but that it would be considered if a similar case happened again.
Apart from the application of the threshold, the team noted that appropriate investigations and reporting were done in the examined OFIS cases.

audits.title: Official controls on animals and goods entering the European Union and verification of compliance of border control posts with European Union requirements

recommendations.text: To ensure that physical checks, and in particular clinical examinations, are carried out on consignments of animals in transit in accordance with the detailed rules for the performance of such checks.

citations.text: The SFVS stated that consignments of bovine animals in transit are not partially or fully unloaded for identity and physical checks at the BCP of arrival, but that they conduct a visual check of the animals on the means of transport, using fixed platforms. The audit team noted that this does not allow an appropriate clinical examination of the selected 10 animals to be performed, which is not in line with Article 4(3) and Part II of Annex I to Regulation (EU) 2019/2130.

The system in place ensures that consignments of animals and goods entering the EU are presented for official controls, and that those controls are, generally carried out in line with guidelines, documented procedures and Union legislation. A limited number of shortcomings were identified, the most significant of which related to the performance of physical checks on consignments of animals in transit, which are based on a visual check rather than a clinical examination as required.

responses.response: he State Food and Veterinary Service of the Republic of Lithuania acknowledges the recommendations of the Audit team and is committed to taking immediate action to ensure live animal checks, as stipulated in Article 4(3) of Regulation (EU) 2019/2130. We would like to address the following issues brought to our attention: According to Regulation (EU) 2019/2130, the same control procedures are required for live animals entering EU Member States as well as for transit through the EU territory. recommendations.text: Ensure that penalties applied to infringements are effective, proportionate and dissuasive as required by Article 139 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: Where the CAs establish non-compliances, the operator receives an official warning containing the consequences of further non-compliances or shall pay a penalty of 30- 300. In 2023 and 2024, 23 such warnings were issued for various non-compliances. In the case of repeated infringements, operators shall pay a penalty of 50-550. Only 50% of the penalty shall be paid if it is paid within 14 days. In the last two years, penalties of 15, 25, 50 and 300 were imposed in six cases. However, such penalties are not effective, proportionate and dissuasive when producers knowingly break official eradication measures of an outbreak, such as by planting potatoes in infected or potentially infected fields or by planting uncertified tubers in other sites of a DA (see also finding 30). The applied penalties are not in line with Article 139 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The situation did not change since 2018 when the CA had already been recommended to implement dissuasive sanctions in case of infringements with regard to the application of phytosanitary measures. An amendment of the Phytosanitary Act was in public consultation in the beginning of 2025 and this was intended to increase sanctions. 5.1.4 Laboratories

audits.title: evaluate the implementation of official controls on feed hygiene

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls consistently verify that feed business operators meet the requirements for appropriate checks of the effectiveness of measures they have taken to minimise cross-contamination.
recommendations.legal_basis: point 2(b) of the section "Facilities and equipment" 3 of the section "Production" of Annex II to Regulation (EC) 183/2005

citations.text: Verification of an establishment's tests to evaluate measures designed to minimise cross-contamination, as required by point 2(b) of the "Facilities and Equipment" section and point 3 of the "Production" section of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005, is an integral component of inspections, when applicable. In all three establishments visited, the operator's test procedures and related test reports were available. In one establishment, the incremental samples collected were pooled and incorrectly sent as one sample to the laboratory for analysis. In another establishment, 15 incremental samples were collected to check the potential cross-contamination, but all these samples were collected from the first mix after cleaning, whilst the production batch contained 10-15 mixes. In another establishment, the results of the cross-contamination tests were higher than the target described in the operational procedure. In two establishments, no evidence was available that the physical attribution of the tracers used during the tests is similar to the coccidiostats used during production. These shortcomings were overlooked during previous official inspections, putting into question the effectiveness of checks carried out on this aspect. The feed inspectors met by the audit team experienced difficulties in comprehensively assessing the procedures and the results of the cross-contamination tests.

The system of planning of inspections is based on appropriate risk-related factors and ensures that the official inspections are carried out regularly, on a risk-basis and with appropriate frequency. While feed inspectors regularly use checklists and guidance documents and official inspections are documented, the effectiveness of these inspections is weakened by shortcomings in the inspectors' assessment of FeBOs tests on cross-contamination. 5.2.2 Sampling and analysis 5.2.2.1 Planning of official sampling

recommendations.text: To ensure that the competent authorities' samplers have appropriate equipment (i.e. a mechanical or automatic divider necessary for preparation of final samples in case of the control of constituents or substances likely to be distributed non-uniformly in feed), and consistently apply sampling techniques ensuring official samples' legal and technical validity.

citations.text: The audit team observed official sampling in two compound feed manufacturers visited (the matrix and parameters to be controlled were suggested by the audit team). In both cases, the distribution of the potential contamination was heterogeneous in the matrix and inspectors sampled a part of the batch (sampled portion). The audit team identified several shortcomings during the official sampling: · the inaccurate calculation of the number of the incremental samples; · the inappropriate mixing of the aggregate, reduced and final samples; · the inappropriate reduction of aggregate sample to reduced sample and reduced sample to final samples (using dividers); · limited knowledge on the concept and calculation of sampled portion. These are not in line with the legal requirements of Annex I to Regulation (EC) 152/2009.

SFVS officials and local feed inspectors stated that they do not have dividers that could be used during official sampling when the contamination is heterogeneously distributed in the sampled feed. This is not in line with the requirements of point 9.4 of Annex I to Regulation (EC) 152/2009. 5.2.2.3 Testing of official feed samples

Many aspects of the planning and implementation of sampling and testing of official feed samples are positive. A risk-based approach has been adopted for the planning of official sampling, and the interpretation of the analytical results is correct. However, the inappropriate official sampling could adversely affect the legal and technical validity of official feed samples, and the reliability of decisions made on the basis of the corresponding results. 5.2.3 Actions taken on non-compliances

audits.title: Meat preparations and meat products

recommendations.text: In order to meet the requirements of Article 148 (3) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, the CAs should ensure that establishments are approved for the activities concerned only if the food business operator has demonstrated that it complies with the relevant requirements of food law.

citations.text: The audit team noted in all the establishments visited that they were approved for all the activities carried out. However, one of the establishments visited by the audit team was approved to produce meat products and meat preparations, despite the fact that the production of meat preparations had not been carried out for several years (no facilities, equipment and HACCP plan were available). The CA had not withdrawn the approval for this activity. Conclusions on approval of establishments

Specific procedures for the approval of food business establishments are in place, enabling the competent authorities to maintain oversight and to take appropriate actions when the conditions are no longer met. However, the shortcomings noted during the audit show that they are not always properly implemented, compromising the guarantees that approved establishments comply with the relevant requirements of EU food law.

Concerning the situation described above, the audit team noted that the problem arose from the fact that the premises were not adequate for the volume of production of the establishment (according to the FBO the current throughput of RTE products was 423 tons per month). To confirm if this was the case, the audit team requested from the CA the production capacity that was declared by the FBO at the time of approval of the establishment, as this aspect should also be checked during the controls (see paragraphs 25 and 29). The SFVS was unable to provide this information and acknowledged that these data are not easily available from the database to the CA staff and may therefore cause difficulties to the staff to perform their verification during inspections/audits.

recommendations.text: In order to perform their duties competently and in a consistent manner, the CCA should ensure, in line with the provisions of point 4 of Article 5 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, that the official control staff receive the necessary additional training and support, for carrying out their control duties in establishments producing meat products. In particular, the CCA should provide the control staff involved in official controls of meat products establishments producing RTE foods with training and guidance (as necessary): · on the relevant requirements of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005, and · on the requirements related to the official controls on FBOs' procedures based on HACCP principles. The CAs should verify that FBOs fulfil their obligations, as specified in Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 and Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. This includes verifying the adequacy of procedures based on HACCP principles to effectively manage microbiological risks related to ready-to-eat meat products and ensuring that the physico-chemical evaluation of these products, to assess their ability to support Listeria monocytogenes growth, is conducted correctly.

citations.text: Evidence was provided to the audit team of staff participation in training sessions that are particularly relevant for carrying out official controls on production of meat preparations and meat products in all the regions visited. However, in certain areas - mainly in relation to Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point (HACCP) requirements and some of the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005, which have an impact on the effectiveness of official controls over the production of ready-to-eat (RTE) food - the audit team found gaps in CA inspection staff knowledge (see also paragraphs 50 and 52).

Although a training system is in place, covering topics pertinent to the sector audited, the observed gaps in the CA's knowledge of HACCP requirements and to the applicable microbiological criteria for Listeria monocytogenes in RTE meat products raise doubts about its effectiveness, thus jeopardizing the quality of the official controls.

The audit team noted that the non-compliances detected by the CA auditors were mainly related to the pre-requisite programmes of the establishments (e.g. to maintenance and hygiene issues). This was confirmed by the data provided by the SFVS on the summary of the non-compliances detected in establishments during the HACCP audits in 2024. However, significant non-compliances, not detected during HACCP audits, were observed in the establishments visited: · Concerning the physico-chemical characterisation of a RTE product, which is fundamental to deciding whether it supports or does not support the growth of Listeria monocytogenes. In some establishments, there were no specifications for physico-chemical characteristics of the products and in others, the "product characterisation" was not correct as the FBOs did not consider the inherent variability linked to the product: e.g. intra- and inter-batch variability when testing for pH or water activity (aw). In this regard, it was noted that the guidance document issued by the European Union Reference Laboratory on Listeria monocytogenes (EURL Lm), providing guidance (see: EURL Lm technical guidance document on challenge tests and durability studies for assessing shelf- life of RTE foods related to Listeria monocytogenes) to FBOs and the CAs on how to carry out shelf-life studies, was not known, or in any event, was not taken into account by the CA auditors when assessing FBOs' compliance with the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. · In some establishments, the FBOs used the weight loss of the product during the drying process to demonstrate that the required aw is reached. However, there was no proper validation study to establish correlation between the two values (weight loss and the aw). When available, the validation was based only on one sample or on one product and the result was used for the entire product group (i.e. intra- and inter-batch variability was not taken into account). · In one establishment the FBO could not provide the validation of the cooking step to prove that all the products reached the critical limit temperature.

Listeria monocytogenes sampling and testing included both final products and environmental samples. However, in several establishments visited producing RTE meat products able to support the growth of Listeria monocytogenes, it was noted the following: · Samples from the processing area and equipment were taken mostly after cleaning and disinfection. The EURL Guidelines on sampling the food processing area and equipment for the detection of Listeria monocytogenes recommends that the sampling should be carried out during processing (in order to increase the probability of detecting a persistent strain). Sampling only after cleaning and disinfection makes the detection of the pathogen difficult and can lead to a false sense of security. These aspects were not noted during official controls. Nevertheless, in one of the meat products establishments visited, where the above- mentioned samples were taken also during processing, the audit team noted that the FBO recently, and after the identification of Listeria monocytogenes in the marketplace, participated in a relevant training session provided by a third-party company. · The FBOs tested their products in accordance with the food safety criterion of point 1.2, Chapter 1, Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 using both limits: enumeration with the limit of 100 cfu/g, although no shelf-life studies had been carried out, and for absence/presence in 25g. Footnotes 5 and 7 of Chapter I of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 does not provide for the simultaneous application of both limits. Nonetheless, in the FBOs' interpretation both criteria should apply (100 cfu/g when the product is placed on the market and absence in 25g before the food leaves the immediate control of the FBO). The SFVS confirmed to the audit team that this interpretation is generally used in Lithuania. The audit team noted that FBOs used the limit of 100 cfu/g during and at the end of the indicated shelf life for RTE meat products able to support the growth of Listeria monocytogenes kept under the control of the FBO in the absence of shelf- life studies proving to the satisfaction of the CA that the product will not exceed the above limit.

In addition, the audit team saw examples, when reviewing the CA's follow up actions 11 after RASFF notifications (i.e. when Listeria monocytogenes was detected in RTE meat products), that when another batch of the product concerned was tested for Listeria monocytogenes to prove the safety of the product, the FBO used enumeration with the 100 cfu/g criterion without the FBO's adequate demonstration (i.e. without a shelf-life study) to the satisfaction of the CA that the product will not exceed the limit 100 cfu/g throughout its shelf-life. This is not in line with point 1.2, (in particular the provisions laid down in footnote 5) of Chapter 1, Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005.

The FBOs visited by the audit team did not perform any shelf-life studies for Listeria monocytogenes. The CA highlighted that they only were aware that FBOs in Lithuania in the fish sector carried out shelf-life studies. When discussing the above reported issues with the CA staff and FBOs, the audit team found gaps in their knowledge regarding the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005, in particular related to the studies (including the shelf-life studies) referred to in Annex II to the mentioned Regulation. The SFVS explained that in the SFVS strategic plan 2025-2027, it is foreseen to strengthen communication with FBOs and conduct training/seminars on important topics.

Concerning the frequency of own-check sampling of RTE meat products, the audit team noted large discrepancies: in a large capacity meat products establishment producing over 30 tonnes of meat products on a daily basis, including RTE meat products, the frequency of own-check testing for Listeria monocytogenes is one product from a product group on a quarterly basis while, in a smaller capacity establishment, this frequency was once a month. These frequencies had been accepted, or were not noted, by the CA without assessing how the FBOs made the sampling frequency decision in the context of their procedures based on HACCP principles and good hygiene practice, taking into account the instructions for use of the foodstuff. In this regard, the SFVS informed the audit team that there is no specific guidance available on how to assess the FBOs' own-check sampling plans.

It was also noted that the sampling frequency, for both product and environmental sampling, was not changed (i.e. was not increased by the FBO or the increase was not requested by the CA when the risk changed) even after a RASFF notification related to the detection of Listeria monocytogenes in 25g of one of the RTE meat products.
The audit team noted that during the last years in the establishments visited the own checks meat product and environmental laboratory tests did not identify any Listeria monocytogenes or Salmonella.
